passage:
Joseph, sit with your Ammachi Elizabeth a minute. You remind me of your uncle Benny at fifteen. I'm his mother, so I saw all of it.
The week of the school play, one pimple came up on his nose, and he was certain the whole hall would stare at nothing else. He wore a cap to dinner. Then a girl he liked stopped talking to him, and he said, "Amma, you can't understand. No one has ever felt like this." I didn't argue. He wasn't ready to hear it.
That summer he went to a youth camp in Munnar. He came back talking about a boy from Kochi who had lost his best friend, and a girl who hated her braces. "Everyone's got something," he said, surprised.
The cap went back in the cupboard.

qa.q: Where did Benny go that summer?
qa.a: To a youth camp in Munnar.

qa.q: Why was Benny so sure the whole hall would stare at his pimple?
qa.a: At fifteen he felt as if he were always on a stage with everyone watching, so one small spot seemed huge to everyone else too.

qa.q: What choice did Elizabeth make when Benny said nobody could understand, and why?
qa.a: She didn't argue, because he wasn't ready to hear it; meeting other young people at camp showed him instead.

qa.q: What might Joseph take from hearing about Benny?
qa.a: Joseph might feel less alone, seeing that an uncle who seems settled now once felt nobody in the world could understand him.

grounding: A grandmother tells how her teenage son felt watched and uniquely hurt until meeting others at a camp softened it.

passage:
Rain had soaked Nagpur since morning, and the sole of Hrithik's left shoe had started to flap. New shoes would have to wait until his father's pay came at the end of the month.
On the walk to tuition, every squelch felt like an announcement. Hrithik was sure the girls at the bus stop were laughing at his feet. Nobody in the history of Class 9 had ever been this embarrassed, he decided.
At tuition he tucked both feet under the bench. Pankaj, sitting beside him, leaned over. "Yours too?" He lifted his own foot: a strip of tape wound round the toe. Across the room, the new boy from Wardha had plastic bags inside his sandals against the wet.
Hrithik looked at the three pairs of feet and, for the first time that day, laughed.

qa.q: What did Pankaj have round the toe of his shoe?
qa.a: A strip of tape.

qa.q: Why was Hrithik sure the girls at the bus stop were laughing at his feet?
qa.a: Ashamed of the flapping sole, Hrithik felt as if every eye was on him, so any laughter nearby seemed to be about his shoe 😰

qa.q: What turning point eased Hrithik's embarrassment?
qa.a: Seeing Pankaj's taped shoe and the plastic bags in the new boy's sandals showed him he wasn't the only one.

qa.q: Why might Pankaj have chosen to show his own taped shoe?
qa.a: Pankaj may have noticed Hrithik hiding his feet and wanted him to know it happens to others too, easing the shame without a speech.

grounding: A fourteen-year-old boy on a rainy day feels that everyone is watching his broken shoe and that no one has felt this before, until he sees classmates in the same spot.

passage:
Vaibhav, sixteen, kept his poems in a locked folder on his phone. Nobody, he was sure, had ever felt as alone in a crowded Bengaluru flat as he did. When his older sister Yamini dragged him to a Sunday open mic in a Jayanagar bookshop, he sat at the back, certain every head would turn if he so much as coughed.
A college girl read a poem about feeling invisible at her own dinner table. A retired bank clerk read about missing his village. Vaibhav's lips moved along with some of the lines.
In the auto home, he said, "That clerk uncle wrote my poem. Forty years before me."
Yamini kept her eyes on the traffic. "Next month, you read one."

qa.q: Where was the Sunday open mic held?
qa.a: In a Jayanagar bookshop.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav sit at the back, sure every head would turn?
qa.a: At sixteen Vaibhav felt lonely and self-conscious, as if constantly watched, so even a cough seemed like something the whole room would notice.

qa.q: What choice of Yamini's helped soften Vaibhav's sense that nobody felt like him?
qa.a: Taking him to the open mic, where strangers described his own feelings, rather than simply telling him he wasn't alone.

qa.q: How might the retired clerk feel if he knew Vaibhav recognised his poem?
qa.a: He would likely be moved that a teenager heard his own feeling in it, forty years apart 🙂

grounding: A sixteen-year-old boy who feels uniquely alone and watched begins to soften when he hears strangers voice the same feelings.

passage: "Amma, I'm not going to school tomorrow." "Why, Kartik?" "Everyone saw me drop the trophy on stage. Everyone. They're all talking about it." "Everyone?" "The whole school, Amma. Nobody has ever been this humiliated. Ever." "Aparna, didn't you fall off the stage in Class 9?" "Into the flower pots. In a sari. In front of the chief guest." "Akka, that's different. It's not the same for me." "Kartik, how many people mentioned it today?" "...Two. But they were all thinking it." "Or thinking about their own lunch." "You don't understand." Aparna ruffled his hair. "Maybe not. But I still remember the flower pots, and nobody else does." Kartik almost smiled. "The chief guest, really?" "Front row." Rukmini, their Amma, put a plate of murukku between them.

qa.q: How many people mentioned the trophy to Kartik that day?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: Why is Kartik so sure the whole school is talking about him?
qa.a: He feels that everyone is watching him and that his embarrassment is unlike anyone else's, so two comments seem like the whole school.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation for Kartik?
qa.a: Aparna's flower-pot story and her saying nobody else remembers it, which made him almost smile and see others have felt this too.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel sharing her own embarrassing fall with her brother?
qa.a: She seems warm and a little amused, willing to laugh at herself so that he feels less alone.

grounding: A teenage boy feels his embarrassment is unique and that everyone is watching him, and his sister's story begins to soften that.

passage: Last year, when my best friend Bhavna moved to Delhi, I was sure nobody in the history of the world had felt what I felt. I wrote it in a notebook: "No one understands. No one could." Walking into school, I felt every face turn to check whether I looked sad. I even changed how I walked. Then in December I went to an inter-school science camp in Mysuru. On the second night, sitting on the hostel steps, a boy from Hubli said his closest friend had moved to Dubai, and he'd felt everyone staring at him for weeks. Another boy nodded. I just sat there. My exact feeling, in somebody else's mouth. I'm Kunal, and I still have that notebook. It reads a little differently now. Amma calls it her son's tragic-poet phase.

qa.q: Where was the inter-school science camp?
qa.a: In Mysuru.

qa.q: Why did Kunal change how he walked into school?
qa.a: He felt everyone was watching him to see if he looked sad, and believed his pain was unlike anyone else's.

qa.q: What turning point softened Kunal's belief that no one could understand?
qa.a: Hearing a boy from Hubli describe the same feeling on the hostel steps, which showed others had felt it too.

qa.q: How might the boy from Hubli have felt when Kunal sat there listening?
qa.a: He may have felt less alone too, sharing something private and finding that others nodded in recognition.

grounding: A teenage boy looks back on feeling that nobody had ever felt his loss and everyone was watching him, until meeting others softened it.
